title: Toward Training Superintelligent Software Agents through Self-Play SWE-RL
one_liner: Self-play SWE-RL trains a software agent by letting it create bugs, write tests that expose them, and then learn to repair those bugs inside real code repositories.
lead: A software agent can only become much better than its training data if it can generate new learning experiences for itself, because a fixed curated dataset eventually runs out of fresh software situations. That is the starting point of Self-play SWE-RL. Instead of depending on human-written issue descriptions and hand-prepared training tasks, the system enters real repositories, injects bugs, proposes test-suite changes that make those bugs observable, and then learns to repair what it broke. This produces an open-ended stream of grounded software tasks with formal checks from tests and repository state. The central claim is that this self-play loop creates a path toward much larger-scale software learning because the agent no longer waits for humans to supply each training problem.

problem.h2: Why human-curated software training hits a ceiling
paras: Current software agents usually learn from human-made bug reports, labeled fixes, and prepared test commands. That data is valuable, but it creates a ceiling because the number of human-curated examples grows slowly and reflects human choices about what counts as a useful task.

If the goal is an agent that can surpass the scale of human-prepared software supervision, then the agent needs a way to manufacture its own grounded training episodes inside real codebases. Those episodes must still have objective checks. Otherwise the system could reward itself for meaningless changes. The paper proposes self-play inside repositories as that training source.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Train one software agent by letting it inject bugs, write tests that reveal those bugs, and then repair them, so that the repository itself becomes a renewable source of learning tasks.

panels.title: 4. Repair the repository

steps.text: Give the agent access to real source code and dependencies so that the learning task is grounded in realistic software structure.
Modify the code to create a defect because self-play needs a failure that the agent itself can later repair.
Write tests that expose the bug so that the task has a formal success signal instead of a subjective description.

steps.b: Step 4: Train the agent to repair the bug
steps.text: Let the agent inspect files, change code, and rerun checks until the repository passes again.

steps.b: Step 5: Repeat across repositories and bug difficulty levels
steps.text: Accumulate many autonomous training episodes so that capability grows from repeated grounded software work.

paras: The paper changes software-agent training from human-curated bug-fix datasets to a self-play loop where the agent generates and repairs its own repository-grounded tasks.

hidden.name: how much genuinely new software experience the agent can create for itself
paras: The most important quantity is training-task freshness. A fixed dataset eventually runs out of new situations. A self-play system can keep producing new tasks if it can inject diverse bugs, expose them with tests, and repair them correctly.

Freshness matters because software skill grows from encountering many distinct failure patterns. Self-play SWE-RL raises freshness by harvesting learning episodes directly from repositories. The repository is not just an evaluation object; it becomes the generator of new repair tasks.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark conditions where the agent keeps generating new grounded learning episodes instead of replaying a fixed dataset.

reads.html: The main advantage is that the agent can keep creating new software problems for itself instead of waiting for humans to write more examples.
Self-play SWE-RL increases autonomous software-learning experience by generating repository-grounded bug-fix tasks with formal test-based supervision.

paras: Repository work gives the agent a grounded world with strict checks. A code edit either passes the relevant tests or it does not. That makes reinforcement learning practical because the reward can come from real repository outcomes rather than from human preference labels.

The bug-injection step is useful because it manufactures a repair task whose structure is known. Once the system has created a failure and written a test that exposes it, the repository contains an explicit target: restore correctness while satisfying the strengthened test suite. That creates a complete training episode from within the repository itself.

The self-play loop can scale because each codebase contains many possible faults and many possible repairs. This is the core reason the paper connects the method to future superhuman software skill: the training supply is no longer limited to curated human issue reports.

stages.s: inject a bug into the code
write tests that reveal the bug
repair the repository through code edits
use the outcome as reinforcement signal

math.words: Learn a repair policy that maximizes the chance that the modified repository passes the strengthened test suite after the agent has created and then fixed a bug.
symbols: the reward for restoring repository correctness under the strengthened tests
a penalty for long or inefficient repair trajectories
the repository state after the agent finishes its repair attempt
the sequence of edits and checks used during the repair process

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: The agent changes one file and introduces an off-by-one bug.
It then adds a test that fails only when that off-by-one case is present.
During repair, one candidate patch fixes the visible symptom but breaks another test, so the reward stays low.
A second patch restores the original behavior and passes the strengthened suite, so the reward is higher.
Training therefore favors repair trajectories that truly return the repository to a correct state.

math.note: The objective matters because the repository and tests provide the formal signal needed for autonomous software learning.

charts.title: Human-data baseline
charts.note: This baseline depends on human-curated issue data, so it does not generate fresh repository-grounded training episodes on its own.

charts.title: Self-play SWE-RL
charts.note: The method improves benchmark performance because self-play supplies new grounded bug-fix experience instead of relying only on static human data.

items.html: If the agent creates defects that do not resemble real software failures, the training signal will be less useful because it teaches repair on artificial patterns.

items.b: Tests may check the wrong thing.
items.html: A weak or mistaken test can reward superficial fixes because the repository appears repaired while the deeper bug remains.

items.b: Self-play can overfit to its own task mix.
items.html: If the agent mostly creates the same kind of bug, capability may narrow because the training episodes stop being diverse.
The approach works when bug injection stays realistic, tests precisely expose the defect, and many repositories provide varied repair episodes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small training loop over a few sandboxed repositories. Let the agent insert simple but realistic bugs, add tests that expose them, and then attempt repairs. Compare this self-play regime with a baseline trained only on fixed issue-fix pairs. The demo should show higher transfer to held-out repository bugs because the self-play system has seen a larger and fresher set of grounded repair episodes.
demo.metric_eq: repair_success = passed_repair_tasks / total_repair_tasks; freshness = unique_self_play_tasks / total_training_tasks
demo.closing: The demo must show that autonomous repository-generated practice yields better repair skill than training only on a fixed curated set, because it exposes the agent to a larger and fresher supply of grounded bug-fix episodes.
